method: COMPILED FROM 2 SOURCES. S1: QUOTED from Asia–Pacific expert panel (Wong RSM, Jang JH, Wong LLL, et al.), International Journal of Molecular Sciences (MDPI) 'Monitoring and Treatment of Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria in Patients with Aplastic Anemia in Asia: An Expert Consensus' (published 13 November 2024), 21 claims; LICENCE: CC BY 4.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC11594386). S2: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from Singapore haematology expert panel (Goh YT, Yap ES, Tan CW, et al.), Annals of the Academy of Medicine, Singapore 53(6):371-385 (doi 10.47102/annals-acadmedsg.202475) 'Consensus recommendations for optimising the diagnosis and treatment of paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria in Singapore' (published 28 June 2024), 11 claims; LICENCE: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (the journal's licence for all its articles) (read at https://annals.edu.sg/open-access-and-copyright/ (the article page carries no licence line of its own)). Verify each source separately: verify.py --source <file> --only-source S<n>. Edition 2.0 adds S2, the Singapore PNH consensus (Annals, Academy of Medicine, Singapore, 2024): article HTML fetched with curl, scripts, styles, tables and citation superscripts removed, tags stripped, abstract to references kept; paraphrased and hash-anchored. The S1 claims are unchanged from edition 1.0.

claims.claim: **PNH is caused by somatic mutations in haematopoietic stem cells.** Blood cells lose some or all of their complement-regulatory proteins, which leads to intravascular haemolysis, thrombosis and bone marrow failure.
claims.source_text: The root cause of these changes is somatic mutations in hematopoietic stem cells, leading to the complete or partial absence of complement-regulatory proteins on blood cells and subsequent intravascular hemolysis, thrombosis and bone marrow failure
claims.locator: Asia–Pacific expert panel (Wong RSM, Jang JH, Wong LLL, et al.), International Journal of Molecular Sciences (MDPI), 'Monitoring and Treatment of Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria in Patients with Aplastic Anemia in Asia: An Expert Consensus', published 13 November 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11594386/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **PNH clones are common in aplastic anaemia (AA):** across seven studies they were found in 25–62% (median 40%) of patients with AA.
claims.source_text: Across seven clinical studies, the presence of PNH clones was observed in 25-62% (median 40%) of patients with AA
claims.locator: Asia–Pacific expert panel (Wong RSM, Jang JH, Wong LLL, et al.), International Journal of Molecular Sciences (MDPI), 'Monitoring and Treatment of Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria in Patients with Aplastic Anemia in Asia: An Expert Consensus', published 13 November 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11594386/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Clone size tracks the clinical picture.** About two-thirds of clones are small (granulocyte clone usually <30%), seen with marrow failure, without clinical haemolysis and with low thrombotic risk. About one-third are large (usually >50%), with classical haemolytic PNH and a high thrombotic risk.
claims.source_text: The majority (two-thirds) of clone cell populations are small (granulocyte clones usually <30%; mean clone size ~11%) and occur in patients with bone marrow failure/cytopenia (mostly aAA). PNH symptoms and clinical hemolysis are absent, and the risk of thrombosis is low. However, one-third of patients have features of classical PNH with large clone size (usually >50%) and overt PNH symptoms including clinical hemolysis, and a high risk of thrombosis
claims.locator: Asia–Pacific expert panel (Wong RSM, Jang JH, Wong LLL, et al.), International Journal of Molecular Sciences (MDPI), 'Monitoring and Treatment of Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria in Patients with Aplastic Anemia in Asia: An Expert Consensus', published 13 November 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11594386/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Myeloid neoplasia is a late risk:** it was estimated at about 12% of patients with PNH/AA over 10 years, and generally carries a poor prognosis.
claims.source_text: the development of myeloid neoplasia in patients with PNH/aAA is a risk and generally has a poor prognosis. It was calculated to occur in about 12% of PNH/aAA patients over 10 years
claims.locator: Asia–Pacific expert panel (Wong RSM, Jang JH, Wong LLL, et al.), International Journal of Molecular Sciences (MDPI), 'Monitoring and Treatment of Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria in Patients with Aplastic Anemia in Asia: An Expert Consensus', published 13 November 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11594386/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **When to test for PNH (Singapore panel):** Coombs-negative haemolytic anaemia with haemoglobinuria, kidney dysfunction, LDH of 1.5 times the upper limit or more, raised reticulocytes, low haptoglobin or unexplained iron deficiency; unexplained or unusual-site thrombosis (such as cerebral, portal or hepatic veins), or clots despite adequate anticoagulation, especially under 45; and marrow failure (aplastic anaemia, MDS) with signs of haemolysis.
claims.locator: Singapore haematology expert panel (Goh YT, Yap ES, Tan CW, et al.), Annals of the Academy of Medicine, Singapore 53(6):371-385 (doi 10.47102/annals-acadmedsg.202475), 'Consensus recommendations for optimising the diagnosis and treatment of paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria in Singapore', published 28 June 2024, https://annals.edu.sg/consensus-recommendations-for-optimising-the-diagnosis-and-treatment-of-paroxysmal-nocturnal-haemoglobinuria-in-singapore/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Diagnosis is by peripheral-blood flow cytometry.** It needs deficiency of at least two different GPI-anchored proteins in two different cell lines (granulocytes, monocytes, red cells). White-cell (granulocyte and monocyte) results estimate clone size better than red-cell results, which haemolysis or transfusion can distort.
claims.source_text: The diagnosis of PNH requires the demonstration of at least two different GPI-anchored protein (GPI-AP) deficiencies in two different cell lines (among granulocytes, monocytes and red blood cells) … Evaluation of leukocytes (granulocytes and monocytes) produces more accurate estimates of PNH clone size compared with evaluation of red blood cells, as results for the latter can be affected by major hemolysis or red blood cell transfusions
claims.locator: Asia–Pacific expert panel (Wong RSM, Jang JH, Wong LLL, et al.), International Journal of Molecular Sciences (MDPI), 'Monitoring and Treatment of Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria in Patients with Aplastic Anemia in Asia: An Expert Consensus', published 13 November 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11594386/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Match assay sensitivity to the question.** A low-sensitivity assay (detects cells at 1%) is acceptable for classical haemolytic PNH; a high-sensitivity assay (0.01%) is needed to find the small clones seen in AA.
claims.source_text: Low-sensitivity assays (that can detect cells at a frequency of 1%) are acceptable for the diagnosis of classical hemolytic PNH, in which moderate or large clones are typically present; however, high-sensitivity assays (that can detect cells at a frequency of 0.01%) are needed to detect small populations of PNH clones in patients with AA
claims.locator: Asia–Pacific expert panel (Wong RSM, Jang JH, Wong LLL, et al.), International Journal of Molecular Sciences (MDPI), 'Monitoring and Treatment of Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria in Patients with Aplastic Anemia in Asia: An Expert Consensus', published 13 November 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11594386/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **LDH marks intravascular haemolysis:** it can rise up to 4–5 times the upper limit of normal (ULN), and untreated PNH generally shows LDH ≥1.5 times ULN.
claims.source_text: A marked increase in serum LDH (up to 4-5 times the upper limit of normal [ULN]) is seen in intravascular hemolysis (compared with only a small increase in extravascular hemolysis) … In PNH, an increase in LDH to ≥1.5 times ULN is generally seen in untreated patients
claims.locator: Asia–Pacific expert panel (Wong RSM, Jang JH, Wong LLL, et al.), International Journal of Molecular Sciences (MDPI), 'Monitoring and Treatment of Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria in Patients with Aplastic Anemia in Asia: An Expert Consensus', published 13 November 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11594386/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **A normal reticulocyte count does not exclude PNH when AA coexists:** the count is usually raised in PNH, but marrow failure can blunt it.
claims.source_text: In patients with PNH, the absolute reticulocyte count is generally elevated [,]; however, this may not be seen in patients who have both AA and PNH
claims.locator: Asia–Pacific expert panel (Wong RSM, Jang JH, Wong LLL, et al.), International Journal of Molecular Sciences (MDPI), 'Monitoring and Treatment of Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria in Patients with Aplastic Anemia in Asia: An Expert Consensus', published 13 November 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11594386/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Individualise assessment and refer** to a specialised centre with expertise in PNH and AA.
claims.source_text: An individualized approach is required when evaluating patients, and referral to a specialized center with expertise in managing PNH and AA is recommended.
claims.locator: Asia–Pacific expert panel (Wong RSM, Jang JH, Wong LLL, et al.), International Journal of Molecular Sciences (MDPI), 'Monitoring and Treatment of Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria in Patients with Aplastic Anemia in Asia: An Expert Consensus', published 13 November 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11594386/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Also screen selected MDS patients:** those with haemolysis, a hypoplastic marrow or refractory cytopenia.
claims.source_text: Guidelines recommend screening for PNH in MDS patients who have evidence of hemolysis, hypoplastic bone marrow or refractory cytopenia
claims.locator: Asia–Pacific expert panel (Wong RSM, Jang JH, Wong LLL, et al.), International Journal of Molecular Sciences (MDPI), 'Monitoring and Treatment of Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria in Patients with Aplastic Anemia in Asia: An Expert Consensus', published 13 November 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11594386/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **After diagnosis (S2), confirm and stage the haemolysis:** full blood and reticulocyte counts, LDH, haptoglobin, bilirubin, urine haemosiderin, D-dimer and clotting times, creatinine and proteinuria; the direct antiglobulin test is negative in untreated PNH. Image for clots (CT or ultrasound), do echocardiography for pulmonary hypertension and brain MRI for headache or neurological symptoms, and examine the marrow if aplastic anaemia or MDS is suspected.
claims.locator: Singapore haematology expert panel (Goh YT, Yap ES, Tan CW, et al.), Annals of the Academy of Medicine, Singapore 53(6):371-385 (doi 10.47102/annals-acadmedsg.202475), 'Consensus recommendations for optimising the diagnosis and treatment of paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria in Singapore', published 28 June 2024, https://annals.edu.sg/consensus-recommendations-for-optimising-the-diagnosis-and-treatment-of-paroxysmal-nocturnal-haemoglobinuria-in-singapore/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Panel recommendation for AA:** screen for PNH at AA diagnosis. If no PNH cells are found, repeat flow cytometry at least every 2–3 years and check LDH and reticulocytes at every visit. Do on-demand flow cytometry for a high LDH or new significant symptoms such as thrombosis. Once PNH cells are detected, repeat flow cytometry at least yearly.
claims.source_text: Screening for PNH should be performed at the time of an AA diagnosis. During follow-up, monitoring for PNH by flow cytometry should be performed at least once every few years (2-3 years) in AA patients in whom PNH-type blood cells were not detected in the initial analysis. LDH and reticulocytes should be measured at every visit. In the event of a high LDH level (with or without a high reticulocyte count) or the development of significant symptoms such as thrombosis, on-demand flow cytometry should be performed. If testing is negative, return to monitoring via clinical laboratory tests and symptoms. Once PNH-type blood cells are detected, subsequent periodic monitoring by flow cytometry should be performed at least once a year.
claims.locator: Asia–Pacific expert panel (Wong RSM, Jang JH, Wong LLL, et al.), International Journal of Molecular Sciences (MDPI), 'Monitoring and Treatment of Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria in Patients with Aplastic Anemia in Asia: An Expert Consensus', published 13 November 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11594386/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Other guidelines set intervals of** every 3–6 months for at least 2 years, then yearly once stable. There is no consensus on the best frequency.
claims.source_text: There is currently no consensus on the optimal frequency of monitoring for different patient subgroups. Available guidelines recommend intervals of 3-6 months for at least 2 years, increasing to 1-year intervals for patients who are stable
claims.locator: Asia–Pacific expert panel (Wong RSM, Jang JH, Wong LLL, et al.), International Journal of Molecular Sciences (MDPI), 'Monitoring and Treatment of Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria in Patients with Aplastic Anemia in Asia: An Expert Consensus', published 13 November 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11594386/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **A D-dimer can help** detect subclinical thrombosis when LDH is raised.
claims.source_text: In addition, a D-dimer test to exclude active thrombosis may help detect subclinical clots in patients with elevated serum LDH.
claims.locator: Asia–Pacific expert panel (Wong RSM, Jang JH, Wong LLL, et al.), International Journal of Molecular Sciences (MDPI), 'Monitoring and Treatment of Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria in Patients with Aplastic Anemia in Asia: An Expert Consensus', published 13 November 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11594386/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **The 'clinically meaningful' clone-size cut-off depends on the country's reimbursement rules**, e.g. a red-cell clone of 1% in Japan but 10% in many countries.
claims.source_text: the cutoff for a clinically meaningful PNH clone size varies between countries, often depending on national reimbursement requirements. For example, the cut-off in red blood cells is 1% in Japan, but 10% in many countries.
claims.locator: Asia–Pacific expert panel (Wong RSM, Jang JH, Wong LLL, et al.), International Journal of Molecular Sciences (MDPI), 'Monitoring and Treatment of Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria in Patients with Aplastic Anemia in Asia: An Expert Consensus', published 13 November 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11594386/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Subclinical PNH (S2): no treatment, but review every 6–12 months** (less often when stable), because the clone can expand into haemolytic or thrombotic disease; small clones in marrow failure are reviewed on the same 6–12-month cycle.
claims.locator: Singapore haematology expert panel (Goh YT, Yap ES, Tan CW, et al.), Annals of the Academy of Medicine, Singapore 53(6):371-385 (doi 10.47102/annals-acadmedsg.202475), 'Consensus recommendations for optimising the diagnosis and treatment of paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria in Singapore', published 28 June 2024, https://annals.edu.sg/consensus-recommendations-for-optimising-the-diagnosis-and-treatment-of-paroxysmal-nocturnal-haemoglobinuria-in-singapore/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **On eculizumab (S2), check full blood and reticulocyte counts, LDH and bilirubin monthly for the first 3 months, then every 3 months,** and reassess the benefit every 6 months. Stopping may be considered for a non-adherent patient after a full assessment.
claims.locator: Singapore haematology expert panel (Goh YT, Yap ES, Tan CW, et al.), Annals of the Academy of Medicine, Singapore 53(6):371-385 (doi 10.47102/annals-acadmedsg.202475), 'Consensus recommendations for optimising the diagnosis and treatment of paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria in Singapore', published 28 June 2024, https://annals.edu.sg/consensus-recommendations-for-optimising-the-diagnosis-and-treatment-of-paroxysmal-nocturnal-haemoglobinuria-in-singapore/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **C5 complement inhibitors (eculizumab, ravulizumab) are the main treatment for classical PNH.** They are generally indicated for symptomatic patients with haemolysis and high disease activity.
claims.source_text: Complement inhibitors (e.g., eculizumab, ravulizumab) are the main treatment for classical PNH [,]. Treatment is generally indicated for symptomatic patients with hemolysis and evidence of high disease activity
claims.locator: Asia–Pacific expert panel (Wong RSM, Jang JH, Wong LLL, et al.), International Journal of Molecular Sciences (MDPI), 'Monitoring and Treatment of Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria in Patients with Aplastic Anemia in Asia: An Expert Consensus', published 13 November 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11594386/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Subclinical PNH needs no PNH-specific treatment.** When PNH occurs within another marrow disorder, treat the marrow disorder first.
claims.source_text: Patients with subclinical PNH do not need specific PNH treatment. For patients with PNH in the context of another bone marrow disorder, the initial focus is usually on the bone marrow disorder.
claims.locator: Asia–Pacific expert panel (Wong RSM, Jang JH, Wong LLL, et al.), International Journal of Molecular Sciences (MDPI), 'Monitoring and Treatment of Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria in Patients with Aplastic Anemia in Asia: An Expert Consensus', published 13 November 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11594386/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Small clones in AA without haemolysis do not benefit from complement inhibitors;** monitor them for change instead.
claims.source_text: in the absence of hemolysis or PNH symptoms, patients with aAA and smaller PNH clones do not benefit from complement inhibitors but should be monitored for any changes in their disease status
claims.locator: Asia–Pacific expert panel (Wong RSM, Jang JH, Wong LLL, et al.), International Journal of Molecular Sciences (MDPI), 'Monitoring and Treatment of Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria in Patients with Aplastic Anemia in Asia: An Expert Consensus', published 13 November 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11594386/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **If a clone expands in AA and causes haemolysis or thrombosis,** manage it as classical PNH with a complement inhibitor.
claims.source_text: If PNH clonal expansion occurs in a patient with AA, leading to hemolysis or thrombosis, the patient should be regarded as having classical PNH and treated with a complement inhibitor
claims.locator: Asia–Pacific expert panel (Wong RSM, Jang JH, Wong LLL, et al.), International Journal of Molecular Sciences (MDPI), 'Monitoring and Treatment of Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria in Patients with Aplastic Anemia in Asia: An Expert Consensus', published 13 November 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11594386/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Let the dominant problem decide:** if haemolysis predominates, follow PNH guidance; if marrow failure is severe, follow AA guidance even when haemolysis is mild or moderate.
claims.source_text: The treatment of patients with both PNH and AA depends on which condition predominates, hemolysis or bone marrow failure. If hemolysis is predominant, then PNH is the predominant disorder, and treatment guidelines for PNH should be followed. If a PNH clone is present but the degree of bone marrow failure is severe, then regardless of whether hemolysis is mild or moderate, guidelines for treating AA should be followed.
claims.locator: Asia–Pacific expert panel (Wong RSM, Jang JH, Wong LLL, et al.), International Journal of Molecular Sciences (MDPI), 'Monitoring and Treatment of Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria in Patients with Aplastic Anemia in Asia: An Expert Consensus', published 13 November 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11594386/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Eculizumab can be given alongside immunosuppressive therapy:** observational studies found no loss of effect and no safety concerns, whatever the order.
claims.source_text: International and European observational studies found that the concomitant administration of eculizumab and immunosuppressive therapy in patients with concurrent PNH and AA had no adverse impact on the effectiveness of treatment, regardless of the sequence of use, and did not raise any safety concerns
claims.locator: Asia–Pacific expert panel (Wong RSM, Jang JH, Wong LLL, et al.), International Journal of Molecular Sciences (MDPI), 'Monitoring and Treatment of Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria in Patients with Aplastic Anemia in Asia: An Expert Consensus', published 13 November 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11594386/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Allogeneic HSCT can cure PNH but is not first-line** because of transplant-related morbidity and mortality. In AA with PNH it is reserved for severe AA with no other options, after discussion with the patient and family.
claims.source_text: Although it can be curative, HSCT is not a first-line therapy for PNH due to the risk of treatment-related morbidity and mortality … HSCT is an option for patients with severe AA in the absence of any other treatment options. The decision should be made after explanation and discussion with the patient and family. HSCT carries the risk of transplant-related mortality or morbidity; hence, it is generally reserved for cases in which there are no other treatment plans for a patient.
claims.locator: Asia–Pacific expert panel (Wong RSM, Jang JH, Wong LLL, et al.), International Journal of Molecular Sciences (MDPI), 'Monitoring and Treatment of Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria in Patients with Aplastic Anemia in Asia: An Expert Consensus', published 13 November 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11594386/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Vaccinate against meningococcus before a C5 inhibitor (S2):** quadrivalent ACWY plus serogroup B (where available) at least 2 weeks before the first eculizumab dose. Eculizumab raises the risk of life-threatening Neisseria infection, estimated at 0.5% a year (5% over 10 years).
claims.locator: Singapore haematology expert panel (Goh YT, Yap ES, Tan CW, et al.), Annals of the Academy of Medicine, Singapore 53(6):371-385 (doi 10.47102/annals-acadmedsg.202475), 'Consensus recommendations for optimising the diagnosis and treatment of paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria in Singapore', published 28 June 2024, https://annals.edu.sg/consensus-recommendations-for-optimising-the-diagnosis-and-treatment-of-paroxysmal-nocturnal-haemoglobinuria-in-singapore/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Ravulizumab** has about four times eculizumab's half-life, allowing 8-weekly dosing, and in trials it proved non-inferior to eculizumab in controlling haemolysis and avoiding transfusion.
claims.locator: Singapore haematology expert panel (Goh YT, Yap ES, Tan CW, et al.), Annals of the Academy of Medicine, Singapore 53(6):371-385 (doi 10.47102/annals-acadmedsg.202475), 'Consensus recommendations for optimising the diagnosis and treatment of paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria in Singapore', published 28 June 2024, https://annals.edu.sg/consensus-recommendations-for-optimising-the-diagnosis-and-treatment-of-paroxysmal-nocturnal-haemoglobinuria-in-singapore/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Breakthrough haemolysis affects 11–27% of patients on eculizumab.** Once confirmed, raise the dose (for example 1200 mg every 14 days), shorten the interval (for example every 12 days), or switch to ravulizumab, which keeps free C5 lower. Rare C5 variants (mainly in Japanese patients) stop both drugs binding, and C5 inhibitors can leave C3-mediated extravascular haemolysis.
claims.locator: Singapore haematology expert panel (Goh YT, Yap ES, Tan CW, et al.), Annals of the Academy of Medicine, Singapore 53(6):371-385 (doi 10.47102/annals-acadmedsg.202475), 'Consensus recommendations for optimising the diagnosis and treatment of paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria in Singapore', published 28 June 2024, https://annals.edu.sg/consensus-recommendations-for-optimising-the-diagnosis-and-treatment-of-paroxysmal-nocturnal-haemoglobinuria-in-singapore/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Proximal (C3) inhibition with pegcetacoplan targets extravascular haemolysis.** In the 16-week PEGASUS trial it raised haemoglobin by 3.84 g/dL more than eculizumab, and 85% versus 15% were transfusion-free, though 3 of 41 stopped because of breakthrough haemolysis. Oral iptacopan (a factor B inhibitor) was approved on phase II data. The panel's criteria for switching from C5 to C3 therapy are in a table not read.
claims.locator: Singapore haematology expert panel (Goh YT, Yap ES, Tan CW, et al.), Annals of the Academy of Medicine, Singapore 53(6):371-385 (doi 10.47102/annals-acadmedsg.202475), 'Consensus recommendations for optimising the diagnosis and treatment of paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria in Singapore', published 28 June 2024, https://annals.edu.sg/consensus-recommendations-for-optimising-the-diagnosis-and-treatment-of-paroxysmal-nocturnal-haemoglobinuria-in-singapore/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Anticoagulation (S2):** with a large clone and no complement inhibitor, consider primary prophylaxis unless thrombocytopenia or bleeding risk forbids it; it may be stopped once a complement inhibitor starts. After a clot, several guidelines advise long-term anticoagulation, but 3–6 months may be enough when disease is well controlled on a complement inhibitor; consider lifelong treatment with extra risk factors or after a life-threatening clot.
claims.locator: Singapore haematology expert panel (Goh YT, Yap ES, Tan CW, et al.), Annals of the Academy of Medicine, Singapore 53(6):371-385 (doi 10.47102/annals-acadmedsg.202475), 'Consensus recommendations for optimising the diagnosis and treatment of paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria in Singapore', published 28 June 2024, https://annals.edu.sg/consensus-recommendations-for-optimising-the-diagnosis-and-treatment-of-paroxysmal-nocturnal-haemoglobinuria-in-singapore/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Supportive care (S2):** folic acid, vitamin B12 and red-cell transfusion for symptomatic anaemia; oral or IV iron for losses through haemoglobinuria; steroids only short-term, for haemolytic episodes; analgesia for smooth-muscle dystonia.
claims.locator: Singapore haematology expert panel (Goh YT, Yap ES, Tan CW, et al.), Annals of the Academy of Medicine, Singapore 53(6):371-385 (doi 10.47102/annals-acadmedsg.202475), 'Consensus recommendations for optimising the diagnosis and treatment of paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria in Singapore', published 28 June 2024, https://annals.edu.sg/consensus-recommendations-for-optimising-the-diagnosis-and-treatment-of-paroxysmal-nocturnal-haemoglobinuria-in-singapore/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Pregnancy is high risk** (maternal mortality estimated at 12–21%, plus miscarriage and preterm birth). The panel supports eculizumab in pregnancy, with frequent monitoring because higher doses may be needed, and anticoagulation, which may be extended through at least 6 weeks after delivery at the clinician's discretion.
claims.locator: Singapore haematology expert panel (Goh YT, Yap ES, Tan CW, et al.), Annals of the Academy of Medicine, Singapore 53(6):371-385 (doi 10.47102/annals-acadmedsg.202475), 'Consensus recommendations for optimising the diagnosis and treatment of paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria in Singapore', published 28 June 2024, https://annals.edu.sg/consensus-recommendations-for-optimising-the-diagnosis-and-treatment-of-paroxysmal-nocturnal-haemoglobinuria-in-singapore/, retrieved 2026-09-24
